content: Sensitive substrates of the enzyme CYP3A4 may experience increased toxicity or reduced efficacy when co-administered with certain drugs. Atazanavir, for instance, can elevate the toxicity of enfortumab vedotin by altering the metabolism of CYP3A4 in the liver and intestines. This necessitates careful monitoring and caution during use. Enfortumab vedotin, an antibody-drug conjugate, releases monomethyl auristatin E (MMAE) through proteolytic cleavage, and MMAE is primarily metabolized by CYP3A4 in vitro. Atazanavir and enfuvirtide both elevate the risk of immune reconstitution syndrome, requiring close monitoring. Additionally, atazanavir increases the levels or effects of erlotinib by influencing CYP3A4 metabolism, necessitating caution. Similarly, erythromycin (in various forms such as base, ethylsuccinate, lactobionate, and stearate) can increase atazanavir levels by affecting CYP3A4 metabolism, requiring careful monitoring. Atazanavir also raises escitalopram levels, increasing the risk of serotonin syndrome, and enhances the effects of esmolol through pharmacodynamic synergy, which may lead to hypotension, bradycardia, atrioventricular (AV) block, and prolonged PR intervals. Dose adjustments of beta-blockers may be necessary. When co-administered with estradiol (oral or vaginal), atazanavir may increase or decrease estradiol levels due to its effect on CYP3A4 metabolism. Alternatives should be considered if available. Similarly, atazanavir can alter the levels of conjugated synthetic estrogens, esterified estrogens, and estropipate, necessitating close monitoring or therapy modification. Atazanavir increases eszopiclone levels, requiring a reduced starting dose of 1 mg/day. It also raises ethosuximide levels, potentially increasing toxicity. Atazanavir elevates etonogestrel and etoposide levels, necessitating caution. It also increases etravirine levels, requiring close monitoring. Atazanavir may increase or decrease etynodiol levels, necessitating therapy modification or alternative options. It decreases the effects of exenatide (injectable solution or suspension) due to insulin resistance associated with protease inhibitors, which can lead to hyperglycemia. Fedratinib increases atazanavir levels by affecting CYP3A4 metabolism, requiring dose adjustments of CYP3A4 substrates. Atazanavir also raises felodipine and fesoterodine levels, necessitating caution. Atazanavir increases fludrocortisone and flurazepam levels, potentially leading to toxicity. Alternatives to flurazepam should be considered, and benzodiazepine doses may need to be lowered. Atazanavir raises fosamprenavir levels, and both drugs increase the risk of immune reconstitution syndrome. Garlic decreases atazanavir levels through an unknown mechanism, necessitating caution. Atazanavir increases gefitinib levels, which may heighten the risk of adverse effects. Atazanavir and givinostat both prolong the QTc interval, requiring ECG monitoring. Atazanavir decreases the effects of glimepiride, glipizide, and glyburide due to insulin resistance, necessitating caution. It also increases guanfacine levels, requiring a dosage reduction to half the recommended dose for extended-release formulations. Atazanavir raises haloperidol and hydrocodone levels, potentially leading to fatal respiratory depression. It also increases hydrocortisone and hydroxyprogesterone caproate levels, necessitating caution. Atazanavir decreases ifosfamide efficacy by reducing its metabolism to active alkylating metabolites. It increases iloperidone levels, which may elevate atazanavir levels due to iloperidone’s time-dependent CYP3A inhibition. Atazanavir raises imipramine and indinavir levels, with both drugs increasing the risk of immune reconstitution syndrome. It decreases the effects of insulin (various forms) due to insulin resistance, which may lead to hyperglycemia or new-onset diabetes mellitus. Isoniazid increases atazanavir levels, requiring caution. Atazanavir raises istradefylline levels, necessitating dose reduction of sensitive CYP3A4 substrates. Itraconazole also increases atazanavir levels. Atazanavir elevates ivacaftor levels, requiring dose reduction when co-administered with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors. It also increases ixabepilone levels, necessitating caution. Atazanavir decreases ketamine levels and increases ketoconazole levels, requiring monitoring. It enhances the effects of labetalol and lacosamide, necessitating dose adjustments. Atazanavir and lamivudine both increase the risk of immune reconstitution syndrome. It decreases lamotrigine levels by increasing its metabolism, with greater clinical significance when ritonavir-boosted. Atazanavir raises lapatinib levels, requiring caution. Lenacapavir increases atazanavir levels, and their co-administration with cobicistat or ritonavir should be avoided. Letermovir increases atazanavir levels, necessitating monitoring. Atazanavir raises levamlodipine levels, requiring dose reduction and monitoring for hypotension and edema. Atazanavir enhances the effects of levobunolol, necessitating beta-blocker dose reduction. Levoketoconazole increases atazanavir levels, requiring caution. Atazanavir raises levomilnacipran levels, with a maximum dose of 80 mg/day recommended when co-administered with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors. It may increase or decrease levonorgestrel levels, necessitating alternatives. Atazanavir decreases linagliptin and liraglutide effects due to insulin resistance. It increases lofepramine and lopinavir levels, requiring caution. Atazanavir raises loratadine and losartan levels, necessitating monitoring. It increases lumacaftor/ivacaftor levels, requiring dose adjustments when initiating treatment with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors. Atazanavir elevates lumateperone and lumefantrine levels, necessitating caution. It increases lurasidone levels, requiring dose reduction to 20 mg/day and a maximum of 80 mg/day. Atazanavir raises maprotiline and maraviroc levels, necessitating dose reduction of maraviroc to 150 mg BID. It increases mavorixafor levels, requiring monitoring. Atazanavir may increase or decrease medroxyprogesterone levels, necessitating alternatives. It raises meperidine levels, potentially leading to toxicity. Atazanavir increases mestranol and methadone levels, requiring caution. It enhances the effects of metoprolol, necessitating beta-blocker dose reduction. Atazanavir raises midazolam and mifepristone levels, with a maximum mifepristone dose of 300 mg/day recommended for Cushing syndrome. Atazanavir decreases miglitol effects due to insulin resistance. Mipomersen and atazanavir both increase hepatic enzyme levels, requiring liver function monitoring. Atazanavir raises mirvetuximab soravtansine levels, increasing the risk of adverse reactions. Mitotane decreases atazanavir levels, necessitating monitoring. Atazanavir increases mometasone levels (inhaled and intranasal), potentially leading to Cushing’s syndrome or adrenal suppression. Atazanavir enhances the effects of nadolol, necessitating beta-blocker dose reduction. It raises naldemedine levels, requiring monitoring for adverse effects. Atazanavir decreases nateglinide effects due to insulin resistance. It enhances the effects of nebivolol, necessitating beta-blocker dose reduction. Nefazodone increases atazanavir levels, requiring caution. Atazanavir raises nelfinavir levels, with both drugs increasing the risk of immune reconstitution syndrome. Atazanavir elevates netupitant/palonosetron levels, requiring monitoring. It increases nicardipine and nilotinib levels, necessitating caution. Nirmatrelvir increases atazanavir levels, requiring monitoring for adverse events.
